source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition
finding: Separates three things: bias (overall confidence level), sensitivity (how well confidence splits correct from wrong) and efficiency (sensitivity given task performance). Gamma and phi correlations are contaminated by bias and by task performance. The same person looks better on an easy task.
numbers: No single number. Review of phi, gamma, type-2 ROC/AUROC2, meta-d' and M-ratio = meta-d'/d'.
quote: a subject's level of metacognitive sensitivity given a certain level of task performance
limits: Review, not a replication. Notes type-2 distributions are unlikely to be Gaussian (Galvin 2003).
agent_relevance: Report bias, sensitivity and efficiency separately for our agent. Never use one calibration number to judge a confidence signal.

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (Nelson 1984 criterion)
finding: The review revives Nelson's 1984 demand that a metacognition measure have no built-in link to task accuracy. Gamma fails this test because it is contaminated by bias and performance.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Argument from logic and simulation, not a field test.
agent_relevance: When we compare confidence quality across tasks of different difficulty, we need a measure that corrects for difficulty, or we will confuse hard tasks with bad monitoring.

source: Rahnev et al. (2020) The Confidence Database
finding: A public pool of confidence studies gives large-sample checks of old effects. Confidence tracks accuracy for most people, but a small group shows negative estimated sensitivity, largely from noise and design.
numbers: 145 datasets, 8,787 participants, 3,955,802 trials, 18 countries. Accuracy-confidence analysis: 71 datasets, 4,768 participants; 293 had a negative beta. Confidence vs confidence RT: mean r = -.07, SD .24, n = 4,089 (76 datasets).
limits: Mostly lab perception and memory studies. Negative values partly reflect few trials (9.9% of negative cases had under 50 trials).
agent_relevance: Single-run confidence on few items is noisy. Negative sensitivity on a small test should not be read as a broken agent.

source: Guggenmos (2021) Measuring metacognitive performance: type 1 performance dependence and test-retest reliability
finding: On Confidence Database data, no current metacognitive measure is independent of type 1 performance. M-ratio falls as accuracy rises. Log M-ratio removes the slope in the regression (beta 0.01, p = .581) but a small pooled rank correlation stays.
numbers: Total N = 6,912. Hierarchical M-ratio vs d' beta -0.19 +/- 0.05, p < .001. Pooled log M-ratio vs d': rs = -0.073, p = .003.
quote: no current metacognitive performance measure is independent of type 1 performance
limits: Empirical dependency partly reproduced by a model with metacognitive noise. Author says more data are needed to call it absent.
agent_relevance: M-ratio is not a free pass for comparing agents with different accuracy. Stratify by accuracy level or use log M-ratio.

source: Guggenmos (2021) test-retest reliability
finding: M-ratio is unreliable at typical trial counts. Under 400 trials, Pearson test-retest r is at most 0.6. About 400 trials is the recommended minimum. Reliability rises with trial count and with accuracy.
numbers: Real data: r about 0.7 at 400-600 trials and 0.85 at 600-800. Simulation: at 60% correct, r about 0.4 even at 400-600 trials; at 80% correct r about 0.8; at 250 trials and 60% correct, r = 0.2.
limits: Simulation assumes one metacognitive-noise model. Simultaneous choice and confidence reports raised reliability most among task features.
agent_relevance: Any benchmark of our agent's confidence needs hundreds of items near 80% accuracy, or the number will not repeat.

source: Guggenmos (2021) extreme M-ratio values
finding: Raw M-ratio produces impossible values for many people. Regularised versions (bounded, hierarchical) help; log M-ratio can even lower Pearson reliability.
numbers: 2.4% of subjects had negative M-ratio and 4% above 1.5; in studies under 200 trials, 4% negative and 10% above 1.5.
limits: Conservative inclusion criteria already applied.
agent_relevance: Prefer pooled or hierarchical estimates, or model-free AUROC2 with a stated accuracy, over per-item raw ratios.

source: Fleming (2017) HMeta-d: hierarchical Bayesian estimation of metacognitive efficiency
finding: A hierarchical Bayes fit of meta-d'/d' beats standard point estimation when data are limited, avoids edge-correction bias and keeps false positives under control in group comparisons.
numbers: Parameter-recovery simulations; author reports the hierarchical method outperforms standard fits at low trial counts (exact errors not copied).
limits: Method paper by the measure's own proponent. Assumes the meta-d' generative model.
agent_relevance: If we compare two agent variants on few items, a hierarchical estimate is safer than two raw ratios.

source: Mazancieux et al. (2020) Is there a G factor for metacognition?
finding: Settles part of an open dispute on domain generality. With enough people and a hierarchical model, metacognitive efficiency correlates across four tasks, even where first-order performance does not. Average confidence level also correlates across tasks.
numbers: N = 181; four 2AFC tasks (episodic memory, semantic memory, executive function, visual perception). 5 of 6 cross-task correlations in meta-d'/d' significant. Type 1 d': executive 2.58, episodic 1.84, semantic 1.19.
limits: Earlier small-sample work mostly found null correlations, so the result depends on power and on the covariance model. One of six pairs not significant.
agent_relevance: Monitoring skill may transfer across domains in people. For an agent do not assume it: test per domain, as the LLM work below shows domain specificity.

source: Rahnev and Denison (2018) Suboptimality in perceptual decision making
finding: Confidence is systematically non-optimal in people. Overconfidence often appears on hard tasks and underconfidence on easy ones (hard-easy effect). Confidence leans on positive evidence.
numbers: Qualitative review across many studies. Over and under-confidence are stable across tasks within a person (Ais 2015, Song 2011).
quote: confidence ratings are suboptimal in depending more heavily on the positive evidence
limits: Review. The authors note that proving suboptimality needs a known cost function.
agent_relevance: Expect bias that changes with difficulty. A fixed recalibration learned on easy items may fail on hard ones.

source: Rahnev and Denison (2018) dissociations of confidence from accuracy
finding: Many studies show conditions with the same accuracy but different confidence. That fails even the weak optimality test, which needs only a consistent internal cost.
numbers: Qualitative, many studies cited.
limits: Cited from review, not re-run.
agent_relevance: Confidence and accuracy can be pushed apart by surface features. Our agent's confidence needs an independent check, not just its own report.

source: Guo et al. (2017) On calibration of modern neural networks
finding: Modern deeper nets are worse calibrated than older ones. Depth, width, weight decay and batch norm matter. A one-parameter temperature scaling fixes most of it.
numbers: ECE uncalibrated vs temperature scaling: CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 16.53% to 1.26%; ImageNet ResNet-152 5.48% to 1.86%; ImageNet DenseNet-161 6.28% to 1.99%.
limits: Image and text classifiers with softmax outputs. Needs a held-out set to fit T. ECE does not measure discrimination.
agent_relevance: Calibration (bias) can be repaired cheaply; discrimination (sensitivity) cannot. Fit a single mapping on held-out agent runs.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice when the format is right. They can estimate P(True) for their own samples, and this improves when they see many of their own samples first. A trained P(IK) predictor works in distribution but is poorly calibrated on new tasks.
numbers: Models up to 52B. Calibration improves with size and few-shot prompting; larger k helps mainly by improving calibration, not AUROC. P(IK) AUROC rises with model size.
limits: Zero-shot calibration is worse. P(IK) generalises only partly. Older base models, not today's RLHF chat models.
agent_relevance: Seeing several own samples before judging is a form of consistency-based confidence. Supports using samples as evidence.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just ask for calibration
finding: For RLHF chat models the verbalized confidence is often better calibrated than the token probabilities. Asking for several answer options first improves it again (the consider-the-opposite trick from human psychology).
numbers: Verbalized confidence plus temperature scaling often cut ECE by over 50% on ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Claude 2 across three datasets.
limits: ECE only; the paper itself warns a constant 50% guesser has perfect ECE in binary tasks. RLHF worsens token-probability calibration.
agent_relevance: Cheap prompt change (list alternatives, then rate) improves bias. Does not show better discrimination.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Verbalized confidence from LLMs is overconfident, clustered at 80-100%. Failure prediction (AUROC) stays near chance for single verbalized answers. Sampling several answers and measuring agreement beats it.
numbers: Vanilla verbalized: average ECE over 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna; GPT-4 mean AUROC only 62.7%. GSM8K, GPT-3.5: AUROC 54.8% (single verbalized) vs 92.7% (5 samples with consistency). White-box vs black-box gap 0.522 to 0.605 AUROC.
quote: none of these techniques consistently outperform others
limits: Five models, eight tasks. No method wins everywhere; all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks (law, ethics).
agent_relevance: Direct support: agreement between samples is a better confidence signal than the model's own number, especially for arithmetic.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) CoT can look calibrated by flat confidence
finding: Low ECE can be an illusion: if the model says 100% every time and accuracy is high, ECE is small but nothing is learned about which answers are wrong.
numbers: GPT-4 with CoT on GSM8K: accuracy 93.6%, ECE 0.064 by giving 100% confidence to all samples. Confidence stayed in the 80-100% range.
limits: One dataset example, GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Always report a discrimination measure (AUROC2 or M-ratio) next to ECE. Matches the Fleming and Lau split of bias vs sensitivity.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) number of samples and aggregators
finding: Consistency-based confidence improves quickly with more samples and then flattens. Mixing verbalized confidence into the consistency score (Avg-Conf) improves failure prediction; Pair-Rank gives the best calibration.
numbers: Tested M = 1 to 13 samples; marginal gain at larger M. Pair-Rank brought ECE as low as 0.028 on average.
limits: Cost grows linearly with M. Gains vary by task.
agent_relevance: A budget of about 5 samples captures most of the benefit. Good default for the schema's confidence step.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning
finding: Sample many reasoning paths and take the majority answer. The share of paths agreeing with the final answer is highly correlated with accuracy, so low agreement signals low confidence.
numbers: Accuracy gains: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9 points. Consistency vs accuracy shown on GSM8K (Fig. 5); no coefficient given.
quote: self-consistency confers some ability for the model to
limits: Correlation shown in one figure on one dataset, not a calibrated probability. Needs a task with a short final answer to vote on.
agent_relevance: Core of confidence from consistency of samples, by code: count agreement in code, no model call needed.

source: Kuhn et al. (2023) Semantic uncertainty / semantic entropy
finding: Counting different surface strings overstates uncertainty. Grouping answers by meaning before computing entropy predicts correctness better than token entropy, lexical similarity or p(True).
numbers: AUROC for semantic entropy vs number of distinct answers: 0.77 vs 0.66 and 0.83 vs 0.79 on the two QA sets (CoQA, TriviaQA; row mapping from a garbled table). Distinct answers per question, correct vs wrong: 1.27 vs 1.77, and 1.89 vs 3.89.
limits: Open QA with natural-language answers. Needs a meaning-equivalence check (NLI model). Gain over simple answer counting is modest.
agent_relevance: If answers are free text, cluster by meaning before counting agreement. If answers are code or numbers, exact match or test outputs does the job.

source: Kuhn et al. (2023) effect of sampling method
finding: AUROC of semantic entropy is stable to how the answers are sampled, even though accuracy changes when diversity is changed.
numbers: Appendix ablation: sampling method has almost no effect on measured AUROC (specific values not recorded).
limits: Detailed numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Confidence from agreement is robust to sampling temperature choices within a range.

source: Lin, Hilton and Evans (2022) Teaching models to express uncertainty in words
finding: GPT-3 fine-tuned on about 100 questions per sub-task can say how confident it is and the numbers are moderately calibrated under shift. It beats a logit baseline in MSE on a harder evaluation. Evidence it uses latent uncertainty rather than copying human style.
numbers: Fine-tuned on add-subtract; tested on multiply-divide and multi-answer. Table 1 reports MSE and MAD; columns garbled in extraction, so no cell values copied.
limits: Arithmetic suite CalibratedMath only. Fine-tuned, so not a prompting result.
agent_relevance: Calibration of stated confidence is learnable cheaply, but a scaffold without training cannot rely on this.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large language models must be taught to know what they don't know
finding: Prompting alone does not give good calibration. Fine-tuning on a small set of graded correct and incorrect answers gives an estimator that generalises, and one model can estimate another's uncertainty.
numbers: A thousand graded examples with LoRA were enough to beat baselines on ECE and AUROC. A user study shows the estimates change how people use the LLM.
limits: Needs open-weight models and labels. Disputes the claim that prompting is sufficient.
agent_relevance: For a scaffold with no training, this suggests an external learned or code-based check should back up self-report.

source: Yona et al. (2024) Can LLMs faithfully express their intrinsic uncertainty in words?
finding: Models answer decisively even when their own sample agreement is low. Faithfulness (match between hedging in words and internal confidence) sits near the 0.5 floor for all tested models by default. Prompting barely helps.
numbers: Vanilla baseline cMFG close to 0.5 for all models and datasets; no model produced any uncertainty expression with default decoding.
limits: Faithfulness is defined against sample agreement; this is their own metric.
agent_relevance: The wording of an answer is a poor signal. Read agreement from samples, not hedges.

source: Cacioli (2026) Do LLMs know what they know? Measuring metacognitive efficiency with SDT
finding: Applies type-2 signal detection to LLM token confidence. Metacognitive information differs between models and is not predicted by accuracy. The confidence signal has unequal variance. Weakest in Science and Technology for all four models.
numbers: 4 models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Llama-3-8B-Base, Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), 224,000 trials. 1.98-fold range of meta-I2r; accuracy-efficiency rank correlation -0.80 (TriviaQA) and 0.00 (NQ). z-ROC slopes 0.78-1.18. Pre-registered.
limits: Open QA has no 2-choice decision so meta-d' is undefined; author uses model-free meta-I2r instead. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Efficiency is domain-specific for LLMs even though people show some cross-domain generality (b08). Test per domain.

source: Cacioli (2026) retracted earlier result and scorer error
finding: The author withdrew his v1/v2 claim of an inverse accuracy-efficiency coupling after finding a length-biased answer scorer. M-ratio was also pinned near 1 by construction in open-ended QA.
numbers: Scorer missed 53% of one model's human-correct answers and 26% of another's (1,200 human adjudications). Agreement with human labels rose 0.76 to 0.86. Rank correlation moved from -1.00 to -0.80 (TriviaQA) and 0.00 (NQ).
limits: Residual scoring error remains by the author's own statement.
agent_relevance: A confidence benchmark is only as good as its correctness labels. Verify the grader before reading any efficiency number.

source: Cacioli (2026) temperature and abstention
finding: Raising sampling temperature lowers accuracy but leaves metacognitive information near flat for three of four models. Metacognitive information tracks the accuracy gain from abstaining on low-confidence items.
numbers: Seven temperatures tested; rank correlation between meta-I2r and abstention gain = +1.00 across 4 models while accuracy does not track it.
limits: Only four models, so rho = 1.00 means a perfect ranking of four, not a strong effect size.
agent_relevance: Selective answering below a confidence threshold is where a good confidence signal pays off.

source: Servajean and Servajean (2026) Measuring (some aspects of) the metacognition of AI
finding: Shows with real LLMs that AUROC2 can give the opposite verdict to M-ratio when type 1 sensitivity differs. LLMs show real metacognitive sensitivity, M-ratio from about 0.65 to near 0.90.
numbers: GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, Mistral-Medium-2508, 5-point confidence after binary judgment. Across tasks AUC2 vs d' Spearman rs = 0.9, p < 0.002. DeepSeek in task A vs Mistral in task B: Mistral higher M-ratio but lower AUC2. Task A: GPT-5 M-ratio above DeepSeek by 0.16.
limits: Three models, three tasks. Many differences are significant but practically small by the authors' own ROPE test.
agent_relevance: Report M-ratio when comparing agents or tasks of different difficulty; AUROC2 mostly tracks task difficulty.

source: Servajean and Servajean (2026) criterion shift with risk
finding: Second experiment tests whether LLMs shift their decision criterion with risk. The criterion moves in the expected direction under each risk configuration.
numbers: Normalised criterion c' below -0.6 under one risk setting and above 0.6 under the other, for all models and tasks.
limits: Prompted payoff setup, not real stakes.
agent_relevance: Models can be told to be risk-averse and shift their answer threshold; a way to set abstention thresholds.

source: Dai (2026), cited in Cacioli (2026): M-ratios of 0.62-0.92 from prompted verbal confidence
finding: A concurrent study applied meta-d' to LLMs with prompted verbal scales. Only the range was seen second-hand, not the original.
numbers: M-ratio 0.62 to 0.92 (second-hand).
limits: Not opened. Original not located.
agent_relevance: Weak lead; confirm before use.

source: Koriat (2012) The self-consistency model of subjective confidence
finding: Not opened this session (paywalled). Claim to check: confidence is read from the consistency of the answers a person samples internally, not from accuracy. Fits the code-based consistency idea.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Marked unopened so it is not used as evidence.
agent_relevance: Primary human source for confidence from consistency. Need the paper before citing figures.

source: Maniscalco and Lau (2012) A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings
finding: Not opened. Origin of meta-d'. Its properties are described in the opened Fleming and Lau (2014) and Fleming (2017).
numbers: Not read.
limits: Second-hand through b01 and b07.
agent_relevance: Use the measure with the caveats in b04 to b06.
